about: A rewrite of the procps tools (ps, pgrep, pidof, pmap and more) in Rust, aiming to work the same as the originals.

prs.title: pmap takes memory addresses written with 0x
prs.broken: Asking pmap for a range of memory with addresses like 0x1000 failed with a parse error. The original tool accepts them with or without the 0x.
prs.changed: I made pmap drop a leading 0x or 0X before reading an address, for a single address and both ends of a range.
prs.matters: Address ranges copied from other tools work as typed.

prs.title: pidof understands %PPID, so scripts can skip their own shell
prs.broken: Scripts check whether another copy of themselves is running with pidof -o %PPID. The Rust pidof rejected %PPID, so the check always said nothing was running.
prs.changed: pidof now reads %PPID as the process that started it, and other values as before.
prs.matters: Cron jobs and init scripts that guard against running twice work again.

prs.title: ps columns no longer shift when a field is empty
prs.broken: When ps could not fill a field yet, it printed the header but no value, so every value after it moved one column left and the PID showed under the wrong heading.
prs.changed: Such a field now prints a dash, as the standard procps does.
prs.matters: Columns line up, so people and scripts read the right values.

prs.title: ps with blank headers prints no empty first line
prs.broken: Asking ps to hide all column headers still printed an empty first line, so scripts reading the first line got nothing.
prs.changed: When every header is blank, the header line is left out, as in the original ps.
prs.matters: Shell scripts that read a process ID from ps work the same as with the original tool.

prs.title: pgrep --older checks how long a process has run
prs.broken: pgrep --older compared the limit with the time since boot when the process started, so nearly every process matched.
prs.changed: It now compares the limit with the process's real age.
prs.matters: Scripts that pick old processes with pgrep, pkill or pidwait get the right ones, as with the original tools.
